subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Scientific Method and Investigation Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on fair tests, variables, data patterns, reliability, and engineering evidence
description: A source-faithful revision pack about how scientists ask testable questions, design fair investigations, collect reliable data, and explain results using evidence. It covers variables, observations, inferences, control groups, graphs, common misconceptions, and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning for middle school science.

data.sourcePassage: Scientific investigation is a way to answer questions about the natural and designed world using reliable evidence. Scientists may begin with an observation, such as a plant growing better near a window, then turn it into a testable question. They do not just guess or accept a claim because it sounds reasonable. Instead, they make hypotheses, identify variables, collect data, and look for patterns. Investigations are often flexible. New evidence can lead scientists to repeat a test, improve a procedure, or ask a new question.

questions.question: What should a scientific investigation use to answer questions?
questions.modelAnswer: A scientific investigation should use reliable evidence.

questions.question: Name one thing scientists may do after collecting new evidence.
questions.modelAnswer: They may repeat a test, improve a procedure, or ask a new question.

questions.question: Why is scientific investigation described as flexible rather than just a fixed list of steps?
questions.modelAnswer: It is flexible because new evidence may lead scientists to revise procedures, repeat tests, compare results, or ask new questions.

questions.question: How does using evidence make a scientific explanation stronger than a guess?
questions.modelAnswer: Evidence connects the explanation to observations or measurements, while a guess may not be supported by data.

data.sourcePassage: A fair test changes one main variable at a time and keeps other important factors the same. In a sugar dissolving investigation, the independent variable might be water temperature, while the dependent variable is the time it takes sugar to dissolve. Controlled variables could include the same amount of sugar, same amount of water, same cup size, same stirring method, and same type of sugar. If several variables change at once, the result becomes harder to explain because scientists cannot tell which factor caused the pattern.

questions.question: Why does changing several variables at once weaken an investigation?

data.sourcePassage: Data tables and graphs help scientists look for patterns. In one investigation, 5 grams of sugar dissolved in an average of 90 seconds in cold water, 45 seconds in room-temperature water, 23 seconds in warm water, and 15 seconds in hot water. The pattern is that dissolving time decreased as temperature increased. A careful claim would say that higher water temperature decreased dissolving time in this investigation. Reasoning can explain the pattern: warmer water particles move faster and interact with sugar particles more often.

data.sourcePassage: One trial is not usually enough to make strong scientific claims. A single result can be affected by mistakes, unusual samples, or measurement errors. Repeating trials and calculating averages can make results more reliable. Scientists also try to reduce bias by using clear measurement rules, recording all results honestly, and not changing the procedure to favor an expected outcome. Larger sample sizes can also help. In a plant investigation, using several plants in each group is stronger than using only one plant per condition.

questions.modelAnswer: Scientists repeat trials to make results more reliable.
options: To prove the hypothesis before testing

questions.question: Name one way scientists can reduce bias.
questions.modelAnswer: They can use clear measurement rules, record all results honestly, and avoid changing the procedure to favor an expected outcome.

questions.question: Why is using several plants in each group better than using only one?
questions.modelAnswer: Several plants reduce the chance that results are caused by one unusual seed or plant, so the evidence is more reliable.

questions.question: How can an average improve the quality of evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: An average reduces the effect of unusual results or small measurement errors and gives a more representative result across trials.

data.sourcePassage: Engineers use scientific investigation to design and improve products. For example, a helmet company could test which padding material best reduces impact force. The independent variable would be the padding material, such as foam, gel, or air-cell padding. The dependent variable would be the impact force measured by a sensor. Controlled variables should include the drop height, helmet shell, mass, sensor, and room conditions. Evidence from repeated tests can help engineers choose safer designs instead of relying on preference or advertising claims.
